detail:
NIAMS' Raynaud's Q&A makes a distinction that shapes ongoing clinical work: most doctors find Raynaud's phenomenon fairly easy to diagnose, but identifying which form a person has is harder. Physicians distinguish primary from secondary Raynaud's with a complete history and physical examination, sometimes with special blood testing; if the evaluation and testing are normal, the primary form is more likely.

One examination gets special attention: looking at the tissue at the base of the fingernail under a microscope (nailfold capillaroscopy), because abnormal tiny blood vessels there can point toward an underlying connective tissue disease such as scleroderma, in which Raynaud's occurs in more than 90% of people. The practical research and clinical direction is earlier, more reliable separation of the benign primary form from secondary cases that need treatment of an underlying disease.

Tabs is not endorsing or verifying this material. Talk to your doctor about evaluation if attacks begin later in life or change pattern.
sourceVideoTitle: Questions and Answers about Raynaud's Phenomenon (NIAMS)
summary: NIAMS notes that spotting Raynaud's attacks is usually straightforward, while telling the primary form from the secondary form is the harder problem; that is why evaluation centers on history, examination, nailfold capillaroscopy, and blood tests.
takeaways: nailfold capillaroscopy examines tiny vessels at the fingernail base
blood tests look for autoimmune markers of secondary causes
most people have the primary form
later onset or one-sided symptoms prompt a doctor's workup
title: Primary or secondary: the question evaluation keeps asking
